# Concurrent Linked Deque

This example demonstrates `ConcurrentLinkedDeque<E>` as a non-blocking,
thread-safe, unbounded deque. It makes concurrent task claiming and an
illustrative two-ended work-stealing policy observable without treating log
order as a concurrency guarantee.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- distinguish FIFO and LIFO deque operations from priority scheduling;
- explain why concurrent `pollFirst()` calls can claim each deque element at
  most once; and
- describe the simplified local-LIFO, remote-FIFO work-stealing policy and its
  limits around fairness, capacity, and load balancing.

## Prerequisite

Install an
[Oracle Java 8](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java8) JDK
or newer and ensure `java` and `javac` resolve to it in the terminal running
this example.

## The program to inspect

`ConcurrentLinkedDeque<E>` is a non-blocking, thread-safe, unbounded
double-ended queue (deque) in Java’s `java.util.concurrent` package. It allows
concurrent access from multiple threads and supports both FIFO (queue behaviour)
and LIFO (stack behaviour) operations.

Unlike `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`, which only offers FIFO operations,
`ConcurrentLinkedDeque` enables both ends to be accessed. Adding a task with
`addFirst()` places it before tasks already waiting at the head; it does not
order work according to an independent priority. Repeated front insertions can
therefore delay or starve tasks at the back.

| Feature           | `ConcurrentLinkedDeque`                             | `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`        |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Thread-safe       | **Yes**                                             | **Yes**                        |
| FIFO support      | **Yes** (`addLast()` / `pollFirst()`)               | **Yes** (`offer()` / `poll()`) |
| LIFO support      | **Yes** (`addFirst()` / `pollFirst()`)              | No                             |
| Access either end | **Yes** (`pollFirst()` / `pollLast()`)              | No                             |
| Best suited to    | Non-blocking, two-ended task hand-off or scheduling | Standard FIFO processing       |

The first demonstration preloads five tasks, then two workers repeatedly claim
tasks from the head with `pollFirst()`. Each successful removal returns one
element, so a task cannot be claimed twice through that deque operation. The
test verifies that every submitted task is claimed exactly once. The workers’
log order is deliberately not a correctness guarantee.

`ConcurrentLinkedDeque` supplies a memory-consistency guarantee for an element:
actions before a thread places it in the deque happen-before actions after
another thread accesses or removes that element. This is a visibility and
ordering guarantee; it does not make a sequence of separate deque operations
atomic, impose fairness, balance work, or provide capacity limits.

Because the deque is unbounded, a faster producer can grow it until memory is
exhausted. When producers must wait for capacity, use a bounded
`LinkedBlockingDeque` and its blocking `putFirst()` or `putLast()` operations.
If a scheduling policy needs fairness, define and enforce that policy
separately.

The work-stealing demonstration uses a common deque policy: a worker takes its
own newest task from the tail (`pollLast()`), while an idle worker steals the
oldest task from the head (`pollFirst()`) of another worker’s deque. This keeps
local processing LIFO and takes stolen work from the opposite end. It is a
simplified illustration, not an implementation of `ForkJoinPool` or a complete
scheduler.

`Main` invokes the concurrent-claiming and work-stealing demonstrations. The
following classes contain the deque operations discussed above.

```java
package demo;

import static demo.utils.Logs.logHeaderAndJavaVersion;
import static demo.utils.Logs.logSection;

public final class Main {

    public static void main(final String[] args) {
        logHeaderAndJavaVersion("Concurrent Linked Deque");

        logSection("Deque example");
        DequeExample.run();

        logSection("Work stealing example");
        WorkStealingExample.run();
    }
}
```

`DequeExample.java`: explain concurrent `pollFirst()` task claiming and the
completion-count observation.

```java
package demo;

import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedDeque;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

import static demo.utils.Logs.log;

public final class DequeExample {

    public static void run() {
        final Deque<Runnable> deque = new ConcurrentLinkedDeque<>();

        log("Add tasks at both ends (slow tasks to the end and quick tasks to the front)");
        deque.addLast(new SlowTask(1));
        deque.addLast(new SlowTask(2));
        deque.addFirst(new QuickTask(3));
        deque.addLast(new SlowTask(4));
        deque.addFirst(new QuickTask(5));
        log("Deque before processing: " + deque);

        final int numberOfThreads = 2;
        final int numberOfTasks = deque.size();
        log("Process queue using " + numberOfThreads + " threads");
        final int completedTaskCount = processTasks(deque, numberOfThreads);

        log("Completed " + completedTaskCount + " of " + numberOfTasks + " submitted tasks");
        log("Deque after processing: " + deque);
        log("Done");
    }

    static int processTasks(final Deque<? extends Runnable> deque, final int numberOfThreads) {
        /* Only in Java 19 the ExecutorService implements AutoClosable! */
        final ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(numberOfThreads);
        final AtomicInteger completedTaskCount = new AtomicInteger();
        try {
            CompletableFuture.allOf(
                            IntStream.range(0, numberOfThreads)
                                    .mapToObj(i -> CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> {
                                        log("Processing tasks from the head of the queue (pollFirst())");
                                        for (Runnable task; (task = deque.pollFirst()) != null; ) {
                                            task.run();
                                            completedTaskCount.incrementAndGet();
                                        }
                                        log("No more tasks available");
                                    }, executor))
                                    .toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new))
                    .join();
        } finally {
            executor.shutdown();
        }

        return completedTaskCount.get();
    }
}
```

`WorkStealingExample.java`: explain local `pollLast()` versus victim
`pollFirst()`, and explicitly label it as a simplified policy.

```java
package demo;

import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedDeque;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

import static demo.utils.Logs.log;
import static java.util.Objects.requireNonNull;

public final class WorkStealingExample {

    static void run() {
        final Deque<SlowTask> slowDeque = new ConcurrentLinkedDeque<>();
        IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).mapToObj(SlowTask::new).forEach(slowDeque::add);

        final Deque<QuickTask> quickDeque = new ConcurrentLinkedDeque<>();
        IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).mapToObj(QuickTask::new).forEach(quickDeque::add);

        final WorkStealingWorker slowWorker = new WorkStealingWorker(slowDeque, quickDeque);
        final WorkStealingWorker quickWorker = new WorkStealingWorker(quickDeque, slowDeque);

        log("Running both workers using two threads");
        log("Slow deque:  " + slowDeque);
        log("Quick deque: " + quickDeque);
        /* Only in Java 19 the ExecutorService implements AutoClosable! */
        final ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
        try {
            CompletableFuture.allOf(
                            CompletableFuture.runAsync(slowWorker, executor),
                            CompletableFuture.runAsync(quickWorker, executor))
                    .join();
        } finally {
            executor.shutdown();
        }

        log("Both workers are complete");
        log("Slow deque:  " + slowDeque);
        log("Quick deque: " + quickDeque);
    }

    static final class WorkStealingWorker implements Runnable {

        private final Deque<? extends Runnable> localDeque;
        private final Deque<? extends Runnable> victimDeque;

        WorkStealingWorker(final Deque<? extends Runnable> localDeque, final Deque<? extends Runnable> victimDeque) {
            this.localDeque = requireNonNull(localDeque, "The local deque cannot be null");
            this.victimDeque = requireNonNull(victimDeque, "The victim deque cannot be null");
        }

        @Override
        public void run() {
            while (true) {
                log("Taking the newest task from this worker’s deque (pollLast())");
                Runnable task = localDeque.pollLast();

                if (task != null) {
                    log("Running the task fetched from this worker’s deque");
                } else {
                    log("No local tasks available. Trying to steal the oldest task from the other worker’s deque (pollFirst())");
                    task = victimDeque.pollFirst();

                    if (task == null) {
                        log("No more tasks are available");
                        return;
                    }

                    log("Running the task stolen from the other thread’s deque.");
                }

                task.run();
            }
        }
    }
}
```
